title: Set Matrix Zeroes
directAnswer: If any cell is 0, zero out its entire row and column — in place. The trap is that zeroing as you scan corrupts the scan, so you must first record which rows/columns to clear. The progression: O(mn) marker copy → O(m+n) row/col sets → O(1) using the matrix's own first row and column as the marker storage.

remember.pattern: In-place marking using the first row/column as flags
remember.formula:
firstRowZero = any 0 in row 0 ; firstColZero = any 0 in col 0
for i in 1..m, j in 1..n: if M[i][j]==0: M[i][0]=0; M[0][j]=0
for i in 1..m, j in 1..n: if M[i][0]==0 or M[0][j]==0: M[i][j]=0
if firstRowZero: zero row 0 ; if firstColZero: zero col 0
rules: Never zero a cell **while scanning** — the new zeros look like original zeros and cascade, wiping the whole matrix. Mark first, mutate second.
Use **row 0 and column 0** as the marker arrays to reach O(1) space — `M[i][0]` flags row i, `M[0][j]` flags column j.
Cell `(0,0)` is shared by both markers — that collision is why you need **two separate booleans** (`firstRowZero`, `firstColZero`) tracked independently.
Apply the markers to the **interior first** (i,j ≥ 1), then handle row 0 and column 0 **last**, or you'll overwrite the flags before reading them.
Three clean tiers exist (O(mn) → O(m+n) → O(1)); name all three and explain what each tier buys.
whenToUse: In-place grid mutation where one cell's value affects a whole row/column
Interviewer pushes from O(mn) to O(m+n) to O(1) extra space
You can repurpose existing cells (a border, a sentinel row) as scratch storage
A two-phase 'mark, then apply' pattern avoids corrupting an in-progress scan
antiSignals: You're allowed a copy and clarity matters → the O(m+n) sets version is plenty
Mutation must not touch existing cells at all → you need a true copy, O(mn)
The effect is local (single cell) not row/column-wide → no marking needed
Non-rectangular / jagged input → the first-row/col flag trick assumes a clean m×n grid
remember.takeaway: When a problem demands O(1) extra space on a grid, look for storage you already own — here the matrix's own border doubles as the marker array. Reusing the input as scratch (with a couple of booleans to resolve the overlap) is the move that turns O(m+n) into O(1).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise that mutating during the scan corrupts it, and whether you can climb the space ladder from O(mn) to O(1) by reusing the matrix's own first row and column as marker storage.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Zeroing rows/columns immediately on finding a 0 — the freshly written zeros are indistinguishable from originals and the whole matrix collapses to zero. Or botching the (0,0) overlap between the two flag arrays.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name all three tiers, then nail the O(1) version by calling out the first-cell collision explicitly and tracking firstRow/firstCol with two independent booleans handled last.

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` integer matrix, if an element is `0`, set its **entire row and column** to `0`'s.

You must do it ***in place***.

A naive O(mn) extra-space solution exists; a follow-up asks for an O(m + n) solution, and a true ***constant-space*** solution is the goal.
constraints: Mutation must be in place; the O(1)-space solution is the target
understanding: Find every original zero, then blank out the full row and full column each one sits in. The subtlety is timing: you have to decide which rows and columns die based on the ORIGINAL matrix, so you can't blank them out as you go — a newly written zero would trigger more zeroing in a chain reaction.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should newly created zeros also trigger zeroing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the original zeros count. That's exactly why we record positions first and mutate second; otherwise the effect cascades across the whole matrix.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What extra space am I allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Start by clarifying the target. The interviewer will usually push from O(mn) to O(m+n) to O(1). I'll present the ladder and implement the constant-space version.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the matrix rectangular?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, a clean m×n grid. The first-row/first-column flag trick relies on every row having the same length.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the whole matrix be zeros, or have no zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both are valid. No zeros → matrix unchanged. All zeros → stays all zeros. The algorithm must handle both without special-casing.

examples.explanation: The single 0 at (1,1) blanks row 1 and column 1; the four corners survive.
Zeros at (0,0) and (0,3) blank rows/columns 0 and 3; row 0 is fully zeroed, columns 0 and 3 are fully zeroed.
No zeros present, so nothing changes.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach

approaches.name: Marker Copy of the Matrix
approaches.whenToMention: The brute-force baseline — say it to establish correctness, then immediately note its O(mn) space is wasteful for a 2D problem.
hints: The core problem is that zeroing changes the very cells you're still inspecting. What if you read from a frozen snapshot and write into a separate place?
Make a full copy of the matrix. Scan the copy for zeros; whenever copy[i][j] == 0, zero row i and column j in the ORIGINAL.
Because the copy never changes, every decision is based on the original zeros — no cascade.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Copying is m·n cells; each zero can trigger an O(m+n) blanking but total writes are bounded by O(mn). Time O(mn); the copy is a full second grid → O(mn) space.
approaches.explanation:
Snapshot the matrix, then use the frozen copy as the source of truth for which cells were originally zero while writing into the live matrix.

**Why a copy makes correctness trivial.** The only hard part of this problem is that a zero you write looks identical to a zero that was already there. A separate, never-mutated copy removes that ambiguity entirely: you scan the copy (which still shows the original zeros), and every blanking you perform on the real matrix is driven by an original zero. No cascade is possible because the copy never gains new zeros.

**Why it's the natural baseline.** It maps the english statement directly to code — 'for each original zero, clear its row and column' — with zero cleverness about storage. It's the version you can write without thinking, and stating it shows you understand the *cascade hazard* before you optimise the space away.

**Why we don't ship it.** Duplicating the entire grid is O(mn) extra memory, the worst tier of the three. The interviewer will ask for better, and the path down the ladder — sets, then border flags — keeps the same correctness guarantee while shedding the copy.
approaches.insight: The copy exists purely to separate 'reading original zeros' from 'writing new zeros'. Every better approach is a cheaper way to remember which rows/columns must die *without* duplicating all m·n cells — first with sets, then with the matrix's own border.

pitfalls: Shallow-copying rows (copy[i] = matrix[i]) — both point to the same array, so the snapshot mutates too.
Scanning the live matrix instead of the copy — reintroduces the cascade bug.
Treating O(mn) as acceptable when the follow-up clearly wants O(1).

approaches.name: Row & Column Sets
approaches.whenToMention: The intermediate tier. Say 'I don't need a full copy — I only need to remember WHICH rows and columns to zero', which motivates two sets.
hints: You don't need every cell of the snapshot — you only need the set of row indices and the set of column indices that contain a zero.
First pass: scan the whole matrix; for each 0 at (i,j), add i to zeroRows and j to zeroCols.
Second pass: for every cell, if its row is in zeroRows or its column is in zeroCols, set it to 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two full passes over m·n cells → O(mn) time. The sets hold at most m row indices and n column indices → O(m + n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Compress the snapshot down to just the information you actually use: which rows and which columns must be cleared.

**Why two sets beat a full copy.** The marker copy stored m·n values, but the decision 'should cell (i,j) become zero?' only depends on two facts: is row i doomed, and is column j doomed? So you don't need the values — just two index sets. One pass collects every doomed row and column; a second pass blanks any cell whose row or column is in a set. That drops the memory from O(mn) to O(m+n).

**Why the two passes can't be merged.** Same cascade hazard as before: if you blanked cells in the first pass, later cells in that pass would see the new zeros and over-mark. Collecting all the doomed indices *before* writing anything keeps every decision tied to the original matrix.

**Why it's not yet optimal.** For a tall-and-wide matrix `O(m+n)` is small, but the follow-up explicitly asks for constant space. The final insight — that the matrix already contains m+n cells we could repurpose as these two 'sets' — is what collapses this into O(1).
approaches.insight: The leap from the copy is realising you only need the row/column *identities*, not their contents — that's an O(m+n) fact, not an O(mn) one. The next leap is noticing the matrix's own first row and first column are exactly m+n spare cells that can hold those facts.

approaches.name: First Row / Column as Markers (Optimal, O(1) Space)
approaches.whenToMention: The target answer. Frame it as 'reuse the matrix's own first row and column as the two sets', and call out the (0,0) collision before you write a line.
hints: The two sets from the previous approach need m + n slots. The matrix already HAS m + n spare cells — its first row and first column. Can you store the markers there?
Use M[i][0] as the flag for 'row i has a zero' and M[0][j] as the flag for 'column j has a zero'. But the first row and first column overlap at (0,0), so track them with two extra booleans.

Phase 1: scan firstRowZero / firstColZero separately. Phase 2: for interior cells set M[i][0] or M[0][j] to 0 on a zero. Phase 3: apply interior markers. Phase 4: zero the first row/col last, using the booleans.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A constant number of full passes over m·n cells → O(mn) time. Only two boolean variables beyond the input → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Repurpose the matrix's own border as the two marker arrays, using two booleans to resolve the cell they share.

**Why the border is free storage.** The O(m+n) sets needed m row-slots and n column-slots. The matrix already owns exactly that many cells in its first column (`M[i][0]`, one per row) and first row (`M[0][j]`, one per column). Store the row flags down column 0 and the column flags along row 0, and the two 'sets' cost zero extra memory.

**Why (0,0) forces two separate booleans.** Cell `M[0][0]` sits in *both* the first row and the first column, so it can't honestly represent two independent facts ('does row 0 have a zero?' and 'does column 0 have a zero?'). The fix is to pull those two facts out into standalone booleans — `firstRowZero` and `firstColZero` computed up front — and let the border cells `M[i][0]`/`M[0][j]` handle only the **interior** (i,j ≥ 1). This collision is the entire difficulty of the optimal version.

**Why order of phases matters.** Apply the interior markers first (rows 1..m, cols 1..n), because the moment you zero the first row or first column you destroy the flags stored there. So: (1) record `firstRowZero`/`firstColZero`, (2) mark interior zeros into the border, (3) blank interior cells whose border flag is 0, (4) finally zero row 0 if `firstRowZero` and column 0 if `firstColZero`. Reorder these and you either lose the flags early or skip the border itself.
approaches.insight: The optimal trick is recognising you already own m+n spare cells — the border — and can borrow them as marker storage, paying only two booleans to untangle the one cell (0,0) that the row-array and column-array both claim. 'Reuse the input as scratch' is the canonical move whenever an O(m+n)-space grid solution is asked to become O(1).

java.explanation: Two booleans resolve the (0,0) overlap — row 0 and col 0 can't both be flagged by the same shared cell.

java.line: for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) if (matrix[0][j] == 0) firstRowZero = true;
java.explanation: Record row 0's fate up front, before the border gets repurposed as markers.
Mark row i (in column 0) and column j (in row 0) for interior zeros only.

java.line: if (firstRowZero) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) matrix[0][j] = 0;
java.explanation: Blank the first row LAST — doing it earlier would erase the column markers stored there.

Border cells M[i][0]/M[0][j] act as the row/column 'sets' for interior zeros.
Apply interior markers FIRST, while the border still holds them.
Handle the first row/column last using the saved booleans.

diagrams.title: The border as marker storage
diagrams.caption: M[i][0] flags row i; M[0][j] flags column j. (0,0) is shared, so two booleans cover the first row/col.

edgeCases.behavior: Single row: firstRowZero=true (0 at col 1); interior loops never run; final step zeros row 0 → [[0,0,0]].
Single column: firstColZero=true; final step zeros column 0 → [[0],[0],[0]].

pitfalls: Using matrix[0][0] alone to flag both row 0 and column 0 — the overlap loses one fact; you need two booleans.
Zeroing the first row/column before applying the interior markers — wipes the flags you still need to read.
Marking the border for first-row/first-column zeros (i or j == 0) instead of only the interior — corrupts the marker semantics.

commonMistakes: Zeroing rows/columns during the scan — new zeros cascade and collapse the whole matrix.
Mishandling the (0,0) overlap between the first-row and first-column marker arrays.
Applying the first-row/first-column blanking before reading the interior markers, destroying them early.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Mutating during the scan (cascade)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you blank a row/column the moment you see a 0, the freshly written zeros are indistinguishable from originals. Subsequent iterations treat them as triggers and the zeroing spreads until the matrix is all zeros.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Collapsing the (0,0) flags into one cell
commonMistakesDetailed.why: matrix[0][0] belongs to both the first row and the first column, so it can't independently signal 'row 0 has a zero' and 'column 0 has a zero'. Using it for both loses information and mis-zeros a border.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Applying the border before the interior
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The first row and first column store the interior markers. If you zero them out first, you erase the flags before the interior cells get a chance to read them.

patternNote: Canonical In-Place Marking with the Input as Scratch. Same instinct as Game of Life's in-place state encoding.
